extracted.intended_audience: archaeologists, antiquarians, and educated general readers interested in prehistoric mining and North American antiquity
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and observational signs used to recognize, date, and culturally attribute prehistoric native copper-mining sites (particularly Isle Royale) and to link them to the so-called mound-builders and historic Native American groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pit morphology and shallow pits
rubrics_metrics.description: "These mijies are rude, irregularly disposed, shallow pits in the general surface, which ... rarely exceed the depth of ten feet, but in some instances reach the depth of twenty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irregular, shallow pits (typically ≤10 ft, sometimes up to ~20 ft), often located where native copper outcrops or along the strike of a copper-bearing belt; presence of drift-heaps and surface depressions indicating ancient pits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heaps of drift-materials and associated debris
rubrics_metrics.description: Pits are "thrown off into heaps, in which are found, mingled with charred wood and other relics, a great many stone hammers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heaps of excavated material containing charcoal, charred wood, stone hammers and relics are diagnostic of human mining activity and help associate surface pits with prehistoric excavation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hammer-produced copper chips and battered surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of "small, thin chips of metallic copper, of irregular shapes, with concavo-convex surfaces, exactly such as would be produced by battering a small nugget ..." and "hammer-marked and pitted surfaces" on large masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thin concavo-convex chips and battered/pitted copper masses indicate extensive cold-hammering techniques; such chips are a primary indication to prospectors of a nearby large mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of simple, laborious excavation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Miners "resorted to the very simplest and most laborious methods ... using their stone hammers, wielded in the hands alone, sometimes aided ... by the application of heat, and by repeated blows battered and broke away the rock."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of sophisticated mining engineering, presence of direct hand-tool use and occasional heat treatment point to prehistoric/simple extraction methods rather than later industrial mining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large masses showing deliberate hammering shaping
rubrics_metrics.description: Large masses "show the marks of long-continued pounding ... seem to have been beaten up into ridges and points, by hammering alone, for the easier removal of parts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morphology of native copper masses (ridges/points) can indicate intentional reduction strategies used by prehistoric miners to detach and remove portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated artifacts (implements, wooden bowls, paddles, charcoal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Finds include "a gad, a chisel, knives, and arrow-heads," a wooden bowl fragment, timber with axe marks, a wooden shovel/paddle, and abundant charcoal and partly consumed sticks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of tools (metal and wooden), domestic vessels, and charcoal within or near pits supports human mining activity and provides cultural and functional context for the site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation/state of organic artifacts informs antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: A raw-hide string "seemed to possess the fiber and much of the strength of dried raw-hide, a circumstance that will not allow the assignment of a very great antiquity to the date of the last mining."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of preservation of organic materials (raw-hide, wood, bark) can be used to assess relative recency of activity; better-preserved organics argue against extreme antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stone-hammer form and manufacture (withed vs unwithed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hammers "are of various sizes and forms ... generally about five inches in diameter ... not grooved for the reception of a withe" while on the south shore hammers were manufactured and "almost invariably grooved them for a withe."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether hammerstones are grooved (withed) or simple beach-wrought pebbles indicates different procurement/manufacture practices and regional cultural variants in tool construction and use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological provenance of hammer stones
rubrics_metrics.description: Hammers are composed of an igneous rock visually a diabase (or dolerite/gabbro) "which ... forms the coast of the mainland for several miles opposite the island."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying the rock types of hammerstones and their non-local provenance (transported by drift or collected from mainland beaches) informs on raw-material acquisition and site connections to surrounding landscapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional withed hammers indicate cultural links
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally a hammer is found that is "withed — i. e., grooved for the reception of a withe handle," which "allies these miners with those of the south shore of the lake."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of withed (grooved) hammers can be used as a diagnostic link between different mining populations or regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratigraphic context and relation to drift and lake levels for dating
rubrics_metrics.description: The dirt they moved "lies on the drift-clay ... some of the pits are but a few feet above the present lake-level ... during the period of the drift ... the interior lakes ... were much higher than they are now."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pits and moved earth lying atop drift-clay and their elevation relative to historic lake levels are used to date mining as later than the last glacial epoch (post-drift).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poles under detached masses as working evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: One mass was found "sixteen and one half feet below the surface, and under it were poles, as if it had been entirely detached, but it had not been much displaced."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural features such as poles beneath masses can indicate techniques used to detach or support masses and provide behavioral inferences about extraction methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold-working (pounding) vs smelting: metallurgical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Copper implements "sometimes contain small nuggets of metallic silver closely welded to the copper. At no other place in the United States are copper and silver found thus naturally combined. They must have been pounded into shape, since the melting of the copper for casting would certainly have produced an alloy in which the appearance of the silver would be entirely lost."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of silver welded to copper and the form of implements indicate cold-hammering techniques and lack of smelting/metalworking by melting; such metallurgical signatures help assign technology level and cultural attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of exotic materials as evidence of wide trade networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Copper implements from Lake Superior are found in mounds with "mica from the Alleghanies, pearls from the Gulf shores ... and sharks' teeth from the cretaceous beds of the South and West."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-occurrence of regionally sourced materials (copper, mica, pearls, sharks' teeth) in single contexts indicates extensive trade/exchange networks and broad cultural connections useful for cultural attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mound-builder social organization (tribal seats and warfare)
rubrics_metrics.description: Squier and Davis: "there probably existed among the mound-builders a state of society something like that which prevailed among the Indians; each tribe had its separate seat, maintaining ... an almost constant warfare against its neighbors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social organization described as tribe-based with frequent intertribal warfare is a characteristic used in comparisons between mound-builders and historic Native American groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic extent of the mound-builders
rubrics_metrics.description: They "occupied the entire country from Lake Superior ... to the Gulf of Mexico ... and from the Alleghanies ... to the Sierras."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide geographic distribution of mounds and shared artifact types across regions supports identification of a widespread cultural phenomenon rather than isolated groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural economy and homogeneous customs
rubrics_metrics.description: They "were an agricultural people, of generally homogeneous customs, habits, religion, and government, each tribe carrying on a trade with surrounding tribes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of agriculture, domestic settlements, and consistent cultural practices across regions is used to characterize the mound-builders and relate them to historic agricultural tribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of smelting and iron; use of cold-working for copper
rubrics_metrics.description: They "worked copper in a cold state, having no knowledge of iron, nor of the methods of smelting any of the ores of the metals by the aid of fire."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metallurgical absences (no iron, no smelting) combined with cold-working signatures are diagnostic of the technological stage attributed to mound-builders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of earthworks and mounds for warfare and sepulture
rubrics_metrics.description: They "built extensive earthworks and mounds, both for purposes of warfare and for sepulture."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence and form of earthworks and burial mounds are primary criteria for identifying mound-builder cultural activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Osteological markers (platycnemic tibia and humerus perforation) — limited diagnostic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Flattening of the shin-bone (platycnemismni) and perforation of the humerus have been regarded as peculiar to mound-builders, but observations show these traits are not uniform and occur in present Indians and other populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Osteological traits may contribute to assessments but are not definitive alone; their inconsistent occurrence requires cautious interpretation and corroboration with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textile production from bast fibers and preservation by copper salts
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles of cloth found in mounds "are made of the bast-fibers of certain plants, and have been preserved by the antiseptic action of the salts of copper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiber types and preservation mechanisms (copper salts) help identify material culture and associate textiles with copper-use contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pottery characteristics: unglazed, slightly baked, rudely ornamented
rubrics_metrics.description: Pottery from mounds is "unglazed, gray, slightly baked or unbaked, and somewhat ornamented by lines and figures," comparable to pottery made by historic tribes like the Mandan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vessel fabric, firing, and decoration styles provide comparative criteria between mound contents and historic indigenous pottery traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stone tool repertoire and sculptural artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: They "wrought stone, making axes, arrow and spear heads, knives, wedges, pestles, discoidal stones, tubes, pipes, beads ..." and "made rude sculptures, in stone and of burned clay, of animals and of the human face."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence and typology of stone tools and sculptures form a core set of cultural diagnostics for identification and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of alphabetic writing; occasional pictorial communication
rubrics_metrics.description: They "had no knowledge of writing by the use of an alphabet, nor hieroglyphics; but sometimes resorted to pictures to convey information."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of formal writing systems and use of pictographic representation inform interpretations of communication and record keeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of diverse materials for personal adornment
rubrics_metrics.description: They "employed shells, pearls, sharks' teeth, obsidian, copper, silver, steatite, black and mottled slate, mica, coralline limestone, the bones of some animals ... galena and hematite" for personal adornment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemblages containing a variety of exotic and local materials for ornaments indicate trade connections and cultural practices important for attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of elephant/mastodon knowledge as inferred from earthworks and artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides representations of present animals, "the elephant (or mastodon) was also known to them, as evinced by the 'elephant-mound' in western Wisconsin ... and by the discoveries of Dr. Koch ... and by the 'elephant-pipe' lately brought to light in Louisa County, Iowa."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iconography or monumental earthworks depicting extinct megafauna are used as evidence for antiquity and aspects of cultural knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnohistoric accounts corroborating indigenous copper use
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from Verrazzano, Hudson/Juet, Raleigh, De Soto, Allouez and others reporting copper ornaments, copper pipes, and native knowledge of copper localities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic explorers' observations of copper use among Native peoples provide documentary corroboration of indigenous copper-working and mining traditions across time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative continuity between mound-builders and historic Indians
rubrics_metrics.description: The article argues that many characteristics of mound-builders "enable any one to recognize also their belonging to the red-men who were here when Columbus discovered America," concluding that aborigines were the mound-builders and ancient miners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A convergence of archaeological, osteological, material-culture, and historic-evidence criteria is used to support hypotheses of cultural continuity; assessments should weigh all lines of evidence rather than single markers.
